Text | Fanyu Meng

Editing | Er Mu, Fanyu Meng

Last summer I took a trip to Germany and had a hard time talking to the guy at the hotel front desk in German. Partly that was because my German, after a few years of barely using it, had gone downhill across the board. But partly it was because he was wearing a mask and standing behind a protective screen, so I really couldn’t make out what he said: by the time his words reached my ears, little was left but the low frequencies. I couldn’t see his mouth or his facial expressions either. Above the mask, the only part of his face still able to convey anything was his eyes, and he was hardly going to waggle his eyebrows at a stranger. So I thought it was time to share some of the interesting research I have come across this year on how masks affect speech.

In fact, right at the start of the pandemic, an Indian colleague at my company suggested we run some mask tests, which would double as a product demo. Nobody took it seriously at the time, and the idea quietly died. Who knew that papers on the topic would then come pouring out, a few of them in JASA? I can’t produce a paper on it myself, but I can certainly knock out a popular-science piece.

The first two paragraphs have more or less already covered how masks affect speech. Below I’ll go through a few points and share some fun research.

High-frequency absorption

By now just about everyone in the world has worn a mask at some point in the past year, and you will have noticed that your voice sounds “muffled” with one on. A mask acts like a piece of sound-absorbing material. The mouth is the source, the mask absorbs part of the sound it emits, and so the sound that passes through the mask is attenuated to some degree. Because a mask is small, its absorption works mainly at high frequencies, which is why voices sound muffled. And since masks are made of different materials with different acoustic impedances, their absorption varies from fabric to fabric.

Think of the mask as the absorbing material in the middle. The incoming sound is the talker’s voice; the outgoing sound is what makes it through the mask, which is what we actually hear.

The University of Illinois ran a series of experiments on the absorption of masks and found that every mask they measured had a clear effect above 1 kHz, and an even stronger one above 4 kHz. In the figure below, the horizontal axis is frequency and the vertical axis is the gain or attenuation of the sound after it passes through the mask. Without a mask there is no attenuation, which serves as the reference line (the black horizontal line).

These high frequencies are essential for hearing sounds like “s,” “f” and “th” in English. Say Trump, wearing a mask, wants to tell Biden: “Shit, you fxxking thug!” Biden just smiles calmly and replies, “What-Dongmei?” (a nod to the famous scene in the Chinese comedy Goodbye Mr. Loser where a hard-of-hearing old man keeps mangling the name Ma Dongmei).

The research found that surgical masks are the kindest to speech: even if the other person has a heavy accent, you can probably still get the gist. On top of that, while the mask keeps out the coronavirus, it also keeps out whatever they had for lunch -_-

Which masks are kindest to listeners?

To test masks, researchers used both real people and dummies. Real voices are more realistic, but a dummy will tirelessly emit white noise or full-band sweeps, so we can see clearly how a mask affects each frequency or band. Talk about dedication.

The design was surely inspired by the Egyptian pyramids [1]

Impact of face masks on voice radiation [2]

Visual effects

Human progress is obviously not going to be held back by a little mask. Can’t see the other person’s lips because the mask is in the way? Just install Windows on it.

You can see the mouth now, but you still can’t hear the words. Of all the masks, the ones with a little plastic window in front hurt speech intelligibility the most.

Still, windows aren’t entirely useless. A teacher, for instance, could perfectly well wear such a mask in class. Add a well-placed microphone, combine it with the WYSIWYG visualization that Windows provides, and speech intelligibility goes up a whole level. In the figure below, with the microphone at the lowest point of the collar, the mask blocks about as much sound as it does for a microphone 1.8 m away. With the microphone stuck to the face under the mask, reflections increase: the sound pressure level goes up, but because of the distortion the speech is not necessarily any clearer. With the microphone on the forehead or on the collar, attenuation across the band is smallest. Why is that? This brings us to directivity, our next topic.

Directivity

As I mentioned in an earlier article, every sound source has directivity.

A history of acoustics: auralization

Take the violin: in the direction the f-holes face, the radiation is strongest and the sound pressure highest (the darkest color).

The mouth, as a sound source, also radiates with a certain directivity. Put on a mask, and absorption, reflection and the like change that directivity. The figure below compares the horizontal directivity of six different masks at different frequencies. Clear differences appear only from the 3.15 kHz band upward.

Horizontal directivity [2]

In the Illinois group’s study, the masks differed considerably in the vertical direction. Take the mask with a window (green line): with the microphone 1.8 m away, its high-frequency attenuation is severe, but with the microphone at the collar the attenuation drops sharply and it even does better than the other masks. You might object that the collar is only 20–30 cm from the mouth, so of course the attenuation there is smaller than at 1.8 m. But notice that at low frequencies the left and right plots show no obvious difference. So we can take it that both sets of curves are equivalent to a measurement at 1 m, which is what makes the comparison meaningful. I am still curious, though, what you would measure with the microphone in front of the mask at the same distance as the collar, since the transfer functions from the mouth to 1.8 m and to 30 cm are not the same.

Besides making accents and dialects even harder to understand, masks cause real trouble for hearing aid users. That is why hearing aid companies have added a “Mask mode” for talking to mask wearers, which adjusts the gain in different frequency bands. Having seen how differently masks attenuate sound, though, I imagine it is hard for manufacturers to come up with a correction curve that works for everyone.

Finally…

The ultimate purpose of a mask is to stop the virus from spreading. So after all this talk about masks and speech, when it comes to choosing one, go back to what a mask is for. Whether people can understand you is secondary; beating COVID is what the whole world is aiming for. After more than half a year of stubborn resistance, Europe and America have finally embraced masks for everyone. In 2021 I hope for fewer anti-intellectuals, a more slowly mutating virus, and higher vaccination rates and better vaccines. And on this day, as Emperor Trump prepares to abdicate and has been permanently banned from Twitter, I wish for world peace.
